claims.statement: `UseFramework.__init__` creates one `ioc.FrameworkContainer` per instance and binds `self.feature` / `self.app_service` as `functools.partial`s of `ioc.inject_feature_to_bus` / `ioc.inject_app_service_to_bus` over that specific container, so a decorated class registers into exactly one bounded context and the decorators are the public registration surface (declared in `use_bus.pyi`).

Both registration decorators return the decorated class unchanged (no wrapping, proxying or subclassing); instantiation is owned by the container provider, so `framework.feature(DTO)` only records a provider.

`_register_service` normalises its DTO argument with `dto_list = dto if isinstance(dto, list) else [dto]`, so one decorator application binds the same class to several input DTO names; the checked typing example is `@framework.feature([CommandA, CommandB])`.

The internal `DTORegistration` alias admits `str` elements, but the registration loop reads `__name__` off every element and nothing resolves a string to a class, while the public stub narrows the decorator argument to classes or lists of classes — the stub is the accurate contract.

The list form of registration is not atomic: because entries are registered one element at a time in a loop, a duplicate on a later element leaves earlier elements already present in both the layer registry and `dto_registry` when `DTOAlreadyRegistered` escapes the decorator.

Per DTO name, `_register_service` (1) checks the name against the target layer's bus-provider `kwargs` and raises `DTOAlreadyRegistered` including the DTO's `__module__`, (2) debug-logs through the container logger, (3) adds the DTO name to `dto_registry`, (4) adds a `providers.Factory` for the class to the layer registry, and (5) attaches the updated registry to the bus provider via `add_attributes`.

An `ApplicationService` registration creates `providers.Factory(decorated_class, framework_container.feature_bus)`, passing the container's `feature_bus` provider as the handler's first positional argument, which is how `ApplicationService.__init__` receives its `feature_bus` and why the handler holds the same `FeatureBus` the facade uses.

Both registries are keyed by the input DTO class `__name__` and never by the class object, both at registration time and at execution lookup time, so two distinct DTO classes sharing a name collide within a layer.

The duplicate check in `_register_service` reads the bus provider's `kwargs` while the accumulation is written with `add_attributes` and read back from `.attributes` at build time; no test in the repository exercises the decorator-side raise paths (the only `DTOAlreadyRegistered` assertions go through the bus registration API or the cross-layer check), so both reads must be verified against the installed dependency-injector before changing how entries are attached.

Every registry update is a `providers.Dict` whose literal places the new name first and the existing entries second, so when a name is already present the earlier entry is the one that survives the dict merge; the step-1 duplicate check is the intended defence against that.

`FeatureBus.register_feature` / `ApplicationServiceBus.register_app_service` mutate the already-materialised `{name: instance}` dict with the same name-collision guard but bypass the container: they do not update `dto_registry`, the decorator is documented as the intended path, and the test suite uses them to wire fixture buses by hand.

Because `register_feature` / `register_app_service` skip `dto_registry`, a handler registered through the bus API has no DTO class recorded, and introspection silently omits names that are missing from the DTO registry.

`build_root_bus()` runs, in order: push dynamic dependencies onto the registration entries, push error handlers onto the bus providers, set `was_initialized = True`, resolve `dto_registry()`, resolve `framework_bus()`, bind context to handlers, copy log flags, publish the DTO registry onto the facade, then guarantee and start observability.

`was_initialized = True` is set before the facade is assigned, so a first build whose facade materialisation raises leaves the flag `True` with `self.bus` still `None`; the first caller sees the original exception and every later `framework(dto)` raises `SincproFrameworkNotBuilt`.

At build time `_add_dependencies_provided_by_user` checks for `"feature_registry"` in the feature bus provider's `attributes`, reads `attributes["feature_registry"].kwargs`, calls `add_attributes(**dynamic_dep_registry)` on each registered entry, and repeats the same for `app_service_registry`; because it runs only from the build, a rebuild repeats the push.

Registration stores `providers.Factory` objects (`providers.Factory(decorated_class)` for features, with `framework_container.feature_bus` added for application services) and no handler instance exists until that provider is evaluated during the build, so the chain from decorated class to live object runs exclusively through `build_root_bus()` / the lazy first call.

`FrameworkContainer` declares `feature_bus` and `app_service_bus` as `providers.Singleton` and `framework_bus` as `providers.Factory` over those singletons, so a second `build_root_bus()` produces a new facade over the same sub-buses, which therefore keep the registries and handler instances they already materialised; only the observability identity surviving a rebuild is directly asserted by a test, the handler identity following from Singleton semantics rather than from an assertion.

The container also declares `logger_bus`, `observability` and `injected_dependencies`; the first two are supplied per instance by `UseFramework.__init__`, while `injected_dependencies` is declared but never read anywhere in the package — the live dependency path is `dynamic_dep_registry` plus the `DependencyLocator` behind `framework.deps`.

The DTO registry is the one container registry whose values are the DTO classes themselves rather than providers, which is what lets introspection describe a registration as name, class and handler together.

Because the container is created in `UseFramework.__init__`, the Singleton sub-buses are scoped per instance rather than per process: two frameworks in one process share neither `feature_bus` nor `app_service_bus` and do not share an `Observability`, and their registries are disjoint.

A service module must be imported after the instance it registers against exists, because the decorators are bound to one container and nothing in the package walks modules looking for decorated classes; the documented bootstrap shape creates the framework first and imports services afterwards, and an unimported module contributes no registrations, which is the diagnosis `SincproFrameworkNotBuilt`'s message points at.

Error handlers differ from registrations in timing: `add_*_error_handler` may be called before or after the build and assigns straight onto the live buses once `was_initialized and self.bus is not None`, whereas the decorators write into the container and reach a bus only through the build.

The failure-mode inventory is: `DTOAlreadyRegistered` at registration time for a same-layer duplicate (`ioc.py` decorators, and `bus.py` for the bus API), `DTOAlreadyRegistered` at build time when `FrameworkBus.__init__` intersects both registry key sets, the same collision re-checked at every call inside `FrameworkBus.execute`, and `UnknownDTOToExecute` raised by the facade when neither registry contains the DTO name.

The cross-layer collision only becomes detectable at build time because each layer's registration-time check looks solely at its own registry; `tests/bus/test_framework_bus.py` builds that situation through the bus API and asserts `DTOAlreadyRegistered`, and asserts `UnknownDTOToExecute` for a never-registered DTO.

`dependency_injector` is a required runtime dependency that `ioc.py` imports for `containers` and `providers` (plus `Dict`, `Factory`, `Object`, `Singleton`); the adjacent comment records that its abi3 wheel does not declare free-threading support, so importing it on a `python3.14t` interpreter prints a `RuntimeWarning` about the GIL being enabled to load `dependency_injector.containers` and silently re-enables the GIL for the whole process, with additional insight that this is not a bug in this codebase and that regular GIL builds are unaffected.

`sincpro_framework/__init__.py` re-exports only `UseFramework`, `Feature`, `ApplicationService`, `DataTransferObject`, `Middleware`, `logger`, `TypeDTO` and `TypeDTOResponse`; neither `ioc.py` nor the container classes and free functions it defines are part of the runtime public surface.

`UseFramework.__init__` overwrites the container's declared `logger_bus` provider with the concrete instance logger immediately after creating the container, and the container's logger is then used both for registration-time debug logs and as the `logger_bus` argument of the three bus providers; that this assignment (rather than the `providers.Object()` declaration) is what those uses resolve to is dependency-injector's container-attribute behaviour and is not asserted by any test in this repository.

Each registered DTO name gets its own `providers.Factory` entry, so the list form `@framework.feature([A, B])` stores two independent providers rather than one shared object; a class registered for two DTO names is therefore instantiated per name rather than shared, which matters for any per-instance state a handler keeps, and no test in the repository asserts the identity or the count of handler instances — the per-name provider is what the code shows, while the double instantiation is a deduction from dependency-injector's `Factory` semantics.

Because `register_feature` / `register_app_service` never update `dto_registry`, a handler wired that way is absent from `inspector.features()` / `inspector.app_services()` and therefore from the entrypoint catalog, which builds its use-case list from those two functions — the handler stays callable in process yet is never published over the MCP or JSON-RPC entrypoints.
